title: The Dark Side of the “Machine God”: 5 Unsettling Truths About Big Tech’s AI Obsession
content:
Silicon Valley routinely promises a sparkling utopia where artificial intelligence will cure complex diseases, optimize global labor, and render the very concept of money obsolete. Yet behind the polished keynotes and corporate public relations, a far more unsettling reality is taking shape. A small handful of ultra-wealthy tech oligarchs, the heads of Meta, Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI, are making unilateral decisions about the collective future of humanity, operating entirely outside democratic oversight or public accountability.

Silicon Valley routinely promises a sparkling utopia where artificial intelligence will cure complex diseases, optimize global labor, and render the very concept of money obsolete. Yet behind the polished keynotes and corporate public relations, a far more unsettling reality is taking shape. A small handful of ultra-wealthy tech oligarchs, the heads of Meta, Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI, are making unilateral decisions about the collective future of humanity, operating entirely outside democratic oversight or public accountability.

This concentration of power exposes a jarring central paradox: the exact same tech CEOs who claim AI will solve humanity’s greatest challenges simultaneously warn that the technology could trigger civilizational extinction, openly describing their pursuit as “summoning the demon.” Rather than pausing development, these executives have accelerated an apocalyptic arms race to build ultra-powerful systems, framing themselves as indispensable guardians of human survival.

To understand where artificial intelligence is truly taking society, we must look past corporate marketing and examine the underlying worldviews, historical lineages, and material harms driving the tech elite. Moving beyond superficial consumer hype reveals how a toxic mix of fringe ideologies, extractive labor practices, and authoritarian state alliances is steering Silicon Valley toward what critical theorists and legal scholars call “techno-fascism.”

To make sense of Silicon Valley’s relentless drive toward Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) and Artificial Superintelligence (ASI), one must understand the bizarre ideological framework shaping its leaders. Coined by philosopher Emile Torres and computer scientist Timnit Gebru, the acronym TESCREAL encapsulates a bundle of tightly interwoven worldviews: Transhumanism, Extropianism, Singularitarianism, Cosmism, Rationalism, Effective Altruism, and Longtermism.

Dr. Emile Torres highlights a critical historical truth at the heart of this ideology: transhumanism is fundamentally “eugenics on steroids.” Unlike nineteenth-century eugenics, which sought merely to optimize the existing human species through selective breeding, transhumanism seeks to use radical technology to completely replace and transcend humanity, engineering an entirely new posthuman species. Within Silicon Valley AI circles, this hypothetical superintelligence is explicitly referred to as a “Machine God.” Tech CEOs effectively act as high priests, competing to bring an all-knowing digital deity into physical existence.

This radical ideology shapes corporate roadmaps in concrete, disturbing ways:

Sam Altman (OpenAI): In a blog post titled “The Merge,” Altman argued that AI surpassing human intellect is inevitable, framing un-merged human beings as a temporary “biological bootloader” for digital intelligence that will ultimately fade into an evolutionary side-branch. Altman notably paid $10,000 to join a brain-uploading waitlist with Nectome and co-founded a brain-computer interface venture to facilitate digital integration.

Ray Kurzweil & Demis Hassabis (DeepMind): Representing Extropianism and Singularitarianism, Kurzweil champions the doctrine of living long enough to achieve digital immortality, targeting a self-improving “singularity” by 2032. Hassabis, DeepMind’s co-founder, operates under a similar singularitarian impulse to engineer self-evolving intellect.

Eliezer Yudkowsky (Rationalism): A foundational figure in modern rationalist thought who famously posited a utilitarian moral calculation arguing that forcing a single person to endure 50 years of relentless torture is ethically preferable to an unfathomable number of people experiencing the mild inconvenience of a speck of dust in their eye.

Elon Musk (xAI/SpaceX): Demonstrating classic Longtermism, Musk explicitly cites the expansion of the Sun billions of years in the future to justify prioritizing multi-planetary space colonization over addressing immediate, real-world human suffering on Earth today.

”All of these ideologies emerged out of modern transhumanism… an ideology according to which we should develop advanced technologies so that we can radically re-engineer the human organism and ultimately create a new posthuman species… In and around Silicon Valley, extremely advanced AI, so-called superintelligence, is even called the ‘Machine God.’ Which means these Big Tech CEOs, racing to release ever more powerful AI, are effectively casting themselves as priests who bring the Machine God’s power to the world.” — Dr. Emile Torres, Philosopher and Historian

Ultimately, the TESCREAL moral math reduces living human beings to disposable statistical noise. By prioritizing hypothetical trillions of digital beings living in far-future galactic utopias, Silicon Valley executives grant themselves ethical permission to ignore present-day environmental destruction, global labor exploitation, and systemic social destabilization.

While modern machine learning is marketed as objective, hyper-advanced science, its core mathematical architecture is directly inherited from 19th-century eugenics. The foundational statistical tools of modern AI, logistic regression, statistical correlation, and neural network pattern classification, were designed by early British statisticians Francis Galton and Karl Pearson. Both were explicit eugenicists who invented these mathematical formulas specifically to measure, rank, and classify human populations to prove that white, wealthy elites were genetically superior.

This mathematical heritage is deeply intertwined with the institutional birth of Silicon Valley itself:

The Palo Alto System: Railroad tycoon Leland Stanford established a horse-breeding facility in Palo Alto, devising rigorous sprint training for foals to optimize racehorse traits, a logic of biological optimization that established the region’s cultural template.

Academic Sterilization: Stanford University’s first president, taxonomist David Starr Jordan (author of Why Fish Don’t Exist), applied Stanford’s horse-breeding logic to human populations, aggressively advocating for state-enforced sterilization of individuals deemed socially or biologically “inferior.”

The IQ Test: Stanford psychologist Lewis Terman reworked a French educational diagnostic tool to create the Stanford-Binet IQ test, explicitly designed to rank human value early in life and justify preventing low-scoring populations from reproducing.

Transistor Pioneers & Eugenics: William Shockley, whose Nobel Prize-winning transistor research birthed Silicon Valley’s hardware industry, spent his later life asserting that Black people were genetically inferior in intelligence. California ultimately carried out approximately 20,000 forced sterilizations — nearly a third of the U.S. total.

Modern artificial intelligence does not “think” or possess conscious understanding; it aggregates massive datasets to find statistical correlations, classify inputs, and rank outputs. Because machine learning inherits historical human data, it inherently formalizes and amplifies legacy societal prejudices under the cover of mathematical neutrality.

”The story of eugenics has always been one that says: yes, you people who have decided that you’re better than everyone else, well, you’re right. And we can find that in science, and therefore it is somehow just… The basic idea of neural networks is very much about classifying and ranking… The very idea that you can create a technology with superior intelligence already carries the assumption that not only is the machine more intelligent, but that certain people are more intelligent and certain others less so.” — Dr. Dan McQuillan and Professor Dave Karpf

When automated recruitment systems, credit-scoring engines, or predictive welfare screening tools deploy machine learning to sort human beings, they operate as high-tech engines of eugenic sorting. As Meta’s former Vice President of Civil Rights Roy Austin noted, when Amazon deployed an automated hiring algorithm trained on historical employee profiles, the system systematically filtered out female applicants. Because the training data reflected a historically white, male benchmark, the algorithm calculated that women were inherently less qualified — a classic demonstration of automated discrimination (“garbage in, garbage out”).

Silicon Valley presents generative AI as a clean, weightless, digital miracle. In reality, as Microsoft Research scholar Kate Crawford notes in Atlas of AI, tech conglomerates rely on a deeply extractive industry model that operates like historic colonialism, framing public data, human artistic creation, and natural resources as unowned entities waiting to be extracted for corporate profit.

This extraction operates across three distinct supply chains:

Mass Intellectual Property Theft: AI corporations harvest copyrighted literature, artistic portfolios, and private online tracking data across the web without consent or compensation. Anthropic, founded by Dario Amodei (a primary architect of AI “scaling laws”), paid out $1.5 billion in legal damages after illegally pirating copyrighted books to train its models. Anthropic’s data acquisition drive even involved purchasing 166 tons of physical Korean-language books to feed its algorithms, drawing fierce condemnation from Booker Prize-winning author Arundhati Roy and international creators.

Exploited Global Task Labor: The hidden engine of machine learning is not autonomous code, but massive manual human labor. Companies like Scale AI, founded by Alexandr Wang, who became a billionaire at 24 before Meta poured roughly $14 billion into his firm, rely on armies of low-wage workers in the Philippines, Kenya, and Venezuela. Paid pennies per task to label data and filter out horrific, traumatic content (“gluing eyes on dolls”), these workers suffer rampant wage theft and severe psychological trauma without basic labor protections.

Ecological Drain and Local Inequality: Training massive foundation models requires intensive mineral extraction for specialized hardware and drains immense amounts of electricity and local water to cool data centers, driving up utility bills for surrounding communities. Meanwhile, the staggering wealth concentrated at the top of Silicon Valley contrasts sharply with local service workers, many of whom are forced to live in cars, parking lots, or overcrowded apartments while working multiple jobs.

Generative AI is not an immaculate cloud of pure intelligence; it is an extractive machine that bleeds the planet’s ecosystems and human labor force dry to satisfy corporate scaling laws.

Big Tech has largely abandoned its historical posturing as a neutral, liberal political force. Instead, major tech corporations are actively forging a strategic alliance with far-right political movements, military apparatuses, and domestic surveillance agencies, a structural convergence known as Techno-Fascism.

Techno-fascism represents the explicit alliance between monopoly digital capital (led by figures like Peter Thiel, Alex Karp, Elon Musk, and Sam Altman) and nationalist state power. Rather than relying solely on traditional physical coercion, this regime enforces political control through automated mass surveillance, data integration, predictive profiling, and algorithmic discipline.

Defense contractor Palantir, co-founded by Peter Thiel and led by CEO Alex Karp, exemplifies this trajectory. In April 2026, Palantir released a chilling 22-point manifesto summarizing Karp’s book The Technological Republic. Analyzed by researcher Rezgar Akrawi, the document explicitly outlines the theoretical foundation of digital fascism:

Point 1: Asserts that the Silicon Valley engineering elite has a “moral duty” to serve the state’s war machine, converting individual conscience into corporate military capital.

Point 5: Deploys deterministic logic to eliminate moral debate, declaring that “the question is not whether AI weapons will be built; the question is who will build them.”

Point 6: Demands the reinstatement of mandatory military conscription, institutionalizing state coercion in service of geopolitical conflict.

Point 21: Promotes explicit civilizational racism, asserting that “some cultures have produced vital advances while others remain dysfunctional and regressive”, a high-tech revival of the colonial “white man’s burden” used to justify domination.

Palantir translates this ideology into real-world surveillance and military infrastructure:

Mass Deportation Systems: Palantir secured a $29.8 million contract with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to power its Immigration Lifecycle Operating System (ImmigrationOS) and Investigative Case Management system. Palantir also developed the ELITE app, which aggregates financial records, social media activity, home addresses, and emergency room Medicaid data into profile maps to calculate probability scores for tracking and deporting immigrants.

Battlefield Targeting Platforms: Palantir, alongside Google, Amazon, and Microsoft, maintains extensive targeting and battlefield management contracts with military apparatuses, supplying real-time AI decision-making platforms deployed in war zones like Gaza.

State Surveillance Integration: Palantir, SpaceX, and Anduril are frontrunners building military projects like the “Golden Dome,” while collaborating with Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) to create APIs linking Homeland Security systems with IRS tax data to target undocumented residents.

”Palantir is creating digital infrastructure for the multiple forms of state violence and control that contemporary authoritarianism relies on, from the software facilitating mass deportations to the AI wielded in wars against colonized people… As technology scholar Jathan Sadowski writes, ‘From inception, Palantir’s purpose has been to provide… the “ontology layer” of fascism, helping to give its ideological goals a material reality.’” — Alberto Toscano, Author of Late Fascism, quoting Jathan Sadowski

This corporate-state pipeline relies on harvesting massive citizen datasets while bypassing privacy laws. In South Korea, for example, the Justice Ministry granted private tech firms access to a state database containing facial photos of 50 million citizens and 120 million foreigners to train commercial surveillance algorithms without user consent.

In his analysis of digital authoritarianism, philosopher Mark Coeckelbergh adapts Hannah Arendt’s classic concept of the “banality of evil.” Historically, Arendt observed that systemic atrocities are rarely committed by monstrous ideologues alone, but by ordinary bureaucrats blindly executing administrative rules without empathy, moral reflection, or personal judgment.

In the modern digital age, AI automates this moral detachment. By delegating life-altering decisions to opaque algorithms, human managers, state agencies, and corporate executives insulate themselves from moral accountability, treating automated recommendations as unassailable mathematical truth. This structural dynamic shifts society away from constitutional rights and toward “algorithmic governmentality” — a system where populations are quietly sorted, disciplined, and controlled through statistical correlations.

This algorithmic control manifests across everyday life:

Workplace Tyranny: Ride-hailing drivers for platforms like Uber and Lyft report having their accounts automatically deactivated without human review when facial recognition software glitches after a driver shaves a beard or gets a haircut. Fast-food employees face similar automated firings, leaving workers with no human appeal process.

Healthcare Exploitation: Hospitals deploy Palantir’s automated staffing tools to generate chaotic schedules, forcing nurses to work six consecutive days without adequate rest while automatically penalizing staff if their schedules conflict with algorithmic targets.

Predictive Profiling: Public schools and social welfare agencies feed family backgrounds, socioeconomic statuses, and behavioral histories into predictive algorithms. These tools profile children early in life, predicting future academic failure or criminal involvement and preemptively restricting their opportunities.

To deepen this control, technofascism targets human psychology. Drawing on Erich Fromm’s Escape from Freedom, Coeckelbergh notes that modern alienation and isolation create deep psychological anxiety. Where historical authoritarianism offered mass political movements to relieve this anxiety, Big Tech offers synthetic AI intimacy. Mark Zuckerberg’s push to deploy AI chatbots to “fight the loneliness epidemic” by creating artificial friends represents a strategy of hyper-personalized emotional pacification: users submit to algorithmic direction in exchange for simulated empathy.

Furthermore, these systems suffer from severe internal dysfunctions. AI systems generate sycophantic feedback loops, telling authoritarian leaders what they want to hear, while risking complexity collapse, data blackouts, and unmanageable administrative failures.

When public figures like Elon Musk openly declare that empathy is a “fundamental weakness of Western civilization,” they summarize the governing logic of technofascism: human empathy, worker rest, and democratic protections are treated as friction that must be eradicated to maximize corporate efficiency.

Despite the rapid expansion of automated surveillance and monopoly corporate power, public pushback against techno-fascism is escalating across the globe. Tech workers are organizing collective resistance under campaigns like #NoTechForIce, frontline hospital nurses are actively resisting algorithmic workplace surveillance, university students are booing AI-focused graduation speeches off the stage, and local community groups are successfully blocking data center construction to protect their water tables and power grids from soaring utility costs.

At its core, this struggle is a vital fight over human agency. The defining question of our era is whether our work schedules, civil liberties, medical care, and democratic futures will be dictated by proprietary algorithms owned by a handful of billionaires, or governed by human communities exercising democratic control.

Reclaiming human agency requires concrete structural interventions:

Enforcing Strict Liability Laws: Implementing robust regulatory frameworks, such as the EU AI Act, to hold corporate executives legally and criminally liable for algorithmic harms.

Antitrust Enforcement: Breaking up monopoly tech conglomerates that control search ecosystems, cloud infrastructure, and mobile operating platforms.

Technological Disarmament: Banning autonomous, algorithmic targeting systems in law enforcement, border control, and military applications.

Labor Unionization & Democratic Infrastructure: Supporting tech worker unions, protecting whistleblowers, and establishing publicly owned, democratically governed data infrastructure.

author: Thomas More
title: A Guide to the Study of Marx - Max Beer
content:
A short study-circle syllabus on Marx by the socialist historian Max Beer. It was published in 1924 by the Labour Research Department as part of its workers’ education series. It covers three areas: Marx’s general views (class society, the relativity of economic and ethical concepts, the Hegelian inheritance), historic materialism, and political economy, from surplus value to the falling rate of profit. It also includes a short biographical sketch of Marx and a suggested order for reading Capital. It ends with G. D. H. Cole’s practical hints for students and class leaders, and period adverts from the Plebs League and the Communist Bookshop. It is a good example of how Marxism was taught to British worker-students in the 1920s.

Labour Research Department, LRD

author: Black Freighter
title: Anarchism and the Australian Labour Movement: Jean De Lisle's Letter from Newcastle, 25 June 1937
content:
Image: BHP at Port Waratah, Newcastle (University of Newcastle [Australia] Library)

This letter, dated 25 June 1937 and written by Jean De Lisle of Newcastle, NSW describes his involvement in Australian anarchist circles. It is unclear who the recipient was. He discusses the difficulties facing the labour movement, criticising the influence of the Santamaria Catholic faction in the Australian Labor Party and its support for Franco during the Spanish Civil War. He also describes the Communist Party's political compromises and intimidation and harassment by communist militants, whom he calls the 'Knuckle Duster Brigade'. A steelworker at BHP's Port Waratah works, De Lisle mentions his subscriptions to Italian and American publications and expresses interest in forming an anarchist group in Sydney.

The original document can be found attached, and was sourced from the Kate Sharpley Library.

168 King St Newcastle New South Wales Australia June 25 – 1937

I have received word from Fellow Worker A. Westbrook of Sydney that she received a letter from you. I am an anarchist and have been connected with a small Italian group in the North of Queensland. One of the comrades (whose name I will refrain from mentioning owing to the possibility of deportation to Fascisti Italy) is now residing near here, and the last time I called on him he gave me a copy of the paper "Spain and the World"

author: Black Freighter
title: The Melbourne Anarchist Club 1886-1891
content:
Image: Flag carried by JW 'Chummy' Fleming at May Day marches in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. In the collection of the State Library of Victoria.

This article by Samuel Merrifield appeared in the Bulletin of the Australian Society for the Study of Labour History, No. 3 (Nov., 1962), pp. 32-43.

2026 marks 140 years since the formation of the Melbourne Anarchist Club. As the first anarchist organisation in Australia, it could in fact be claimed that this year also marks the 140th year of Australian anarchist organising.

Samuel Merrifield (1904-1982) was a surveyor, Labor politician, and labour historian whose experience of unemployment during the Great Depression was the basis of his entry into politics. He was elected as an ALP member to the Victorian parliament in 1943, serving as minister for public works and later deputy leader of the Opposition in the Legislative Council. He helped found the Melbourne branch of the Australian Society for the Study of Labour History and became a leading collector and preserver of Australian labour history.

The influence of the Club is briefly touched upon by Dr R.A. Gollan (1) but a fuller examination of the members' endeavours appears to be worthwhile and, in spite of the critics, these endeavours similarly appear worthwhile and to have contributed to the development of working class history in Victoria.

During the 1880s there was great activity in the formation of industrial and quasi-political organisation and a not inconsiderable amount of industrial dispute. Of political activity there was little.

The re-forming of the National Political League on 20 January 1886 and the change of name to the National Liberal League, reconstituted the liberal organisations of 1865 and 1877. On 8 December 1885 the Working Mens Political Reform Association was established but only lasted four months during which time its greatest activity was to sabotage the National Liberal League. Half of the W.M.P.R.A. members were to join the Anarchist Club.

The Social Democratic League of S.A. Rosa did not appear until 1889 and the Progressive Political League (the Labor Party) in 1891. The Anarchist Club filled the gap.

In Melbourne the Anarchists were brought together within the Australian Secular Association which had been founded on 1 August 1882. The A.S.A. propagated Rationalism or Atheism, Charles Bradlaugh being greatly esteemed, but Bradlaugh and Jos. Symes, the President and Chief Lecturer of the A.S.A., were anti-socialist and opposed to anarchist philosophy.

The A.S.A. Journal, The Liberator, edited by Symes, provided the means of propaganda and the A.S.A. also the audience, the members coming from small businesses or thoughtful workers, with minds free from the influence of the churches which were mostly conservative in those days.

On 19 October 1884 "D" had written that "all Governments are necessary evils -- all classes should be represented and both sexes. Anarchy begins where the State does not understand its true position and meddles in matters of private concern". (2)

Sixteen months later David A. Andrade and James Donovan had a running debate. Said Andrade: "The ends of the industrial stage can only be achieved by joining the Anarchists and refusing aid to State Socialists. Republicans and Anarchists are all in combination to protect individuals against State interferences." (3)

Donovan replied: "Anarchists like Christians and Socialists are of varying degree and of widely diverse characteristics." (4)

How true this was to be shown later.

From Andrade's quotations it is obvious he was an admirer and part believer of Herbert Spencer's who had been dismayed by Beatrice Webb's marriage to the socialist Sydney Webb.

Notwithstanding Donovan's feeling the Melbourne Anarchist Club was formed on 1 May 1886, after word of mouth had been the means to circularise notice to Anarchists, Communists, State Socialists, Republicans, Democrats, Conservatives, Liberals, Radicals, Nihilists and Royalists, all warmly welcomed.

Nothing narrow-minded about that!

The day of the meeting, 1 May, was interesting as it was the day of the year selected the previous year by the Federation of Organised Trades and Labor Unions (of U.S.A.) to be later recommended and adopted as the day for International Sympathy and the Brotherhood of the Working Classes. This day was specially selected in 1888 as the date of Annual Meeting of the Club and two years later again was selected by the Social Democratic Club (the successor to the Anarchist Club) for a special mass meeting to celebrate in Melbourne the spirit of the first official May Day. I believe these to be more than -mere coincidence and worthy of the attention of Len Fox in his investigation of early Australian May Days. (5)

The first and subsequent meetings until 11 September were held on Wednesday evenings in the Australian Secular Association Rooms, 120 Swanston Street, then between Little Bourke Street and Lonsdale Street. After this date the A.S.A. moved to the "Hall of Science" in Bourke Street East and the Melbourne Anarchist Club moved to Room 9, later Room 7, of the Alexandra Theatre (later burned down) and predecessor of His or Her Majesty's Theatre in Exhibition Street. Here they remained until 7 July 1888 when the Club moved to "The Co-operative Home", the premises occupied by J.A. Andrews in Victoria Avenue Albert Park, until he left in 1889.

The Club met regularly either once or twice a week until 2 March 1889. Sometimes members spoke on Queens Wharf on Sundays.

Declining support led to the Club going into recess for sixteen months, then a reunion on 9 July 1890 gave fresh life until 4 December of that year. However, evidence exists that the Club continued to hold meetings until 1892 in "Liberty Hall" on the premises of the Secretary, D.A. Andrade, who conducted a circulating library and book store at 213 Russell Street. Individuals like Andrews continued activity until 1896 when somebody or someone was still deemed to be affiliated with the Anarchist International." (6)

The Club within a fortnight of its founding issued a prospectus which was read to a meeting of fifty people:

The Melbourne Anarchists' Club extends its greetings to the liberty loving citizens of these young colonies and appeals to them to assist its members in their efforts to remove those public sentiments and public institutions, which have been transplanted here from the northern hemispheres, retard social progress and happiness; and to substitute in their place the enabling principles of Liberty, Equality and Fraternity!

The objects of the Melbourne Anarchists' Club are:

1. To foster public interest in the great social questions of the day, by promoting inquiry in every possible way; to promote free public discussions of all social questions; and to circulate and publish literature, throwing light upon existing evils of society, and the methods necessary for their removal.

2. To foster and extend the principles of Self Reliance, Self Help and a Spirit of Independence amongst the people.

3. To uphold and maintain the principles of Liberty, Equality and Fraternity. By Liberty we mean "the equal liberty of each, limited alone by the equal liberty of all." By Equality we mean "the equality of opportunity for each individual." And by Fraternity we mean "that principle which denies national and class distinctions, asserts the Brotherhood of Man and says 'The world is my country'".

4. To advocate, and seek to achieve, the abolition of all monopolies and despotisms which destroy the Freedom of the Individual and which there by check social progress and prosperity.

5. To expose and oppose that colossal swindle, Government, and to advocate Abstention from Voting, Resistance to Taxation, and Private Co-operation or Individual Action.

6. To foster Mutual Trust and Fraternity amongst the working people of all ranks, and to turn their attention to their common foes: the Priests and the Politicans, and their co adjutors, attacking principles rather than individuals.

7. To invite the co-operation of all, who have realised the innate evils of our governing institutions, and desire their speedy dissolution for the general benefit of Humanity.

8. To promote the formation of voluntary institutions similar to the Melbourne Anarchist Club throughout Victoria and the neighbouring colonies, and, with their consent, to eventually unite with them forming The Australasian Association of Anarchists. (7)

Thus the objects were expressions of liberty, economic demands, the lessening of Government and sentiments of internationalism.

Much, of course, could be added in detailed analysis. One small observation - members were known as "comrades", the term subsequently used for long years in the Labor Party and later Socialist and Communist Parties.

For twenty-one months after the founding, the Club reports appeared in the Liberator, but the continuous and fierce attacks strained the forbearance of the editor, Jos. Symes (also President of the Australian Secular Association) who banned their appearance.

Symes was to later blame the machinations of the Anarchists for the deep and bitter schism which split the A.S.A. Seventeen Anarchist Club members out of twenty-seven checked graduated from the A.S.A. and no person recorded as being a supporter of Symes is recorded as present at an anarchist meeting, while seven of the anti-Symes group are so recorded. However, many more anti-Symes people are not so recorded, and Symes himself was noted for intemperate expression throughout his stormy career.

The Australian Radical published reports of the Club and from April 1887 the Club published a monthly paper Honesty, printed by the Co-operative Printing Coy and described as an outspoken advocate of social reform on the basis of "Justice, Equity and Liberty" in which the editorial "Our Colors" outlined the aims and aspirations of the paper.

Poor J.A. Andrews then as later demonstrated his enthusiasm and his poverty by contributing to the press fund. Fred P. Upham acted as publisher.

The formation of the Club evoked hope and cynicism as reflected in these two verses.

We'll trumpet a note to the heart of men A note to sound in the darkest den Where sorrow and sickness and sin are rife, To peal to the poorest of prostrate souls, And call them back to their own lost right, To blare and burst when the war drum rolls, And riot and ring in the rage of fights. (8)

And now our hopes with great hubbub, Will burn away to embers For the great and good Anarchist Club Has half-a-dozen members. The Government we'll tumble down The soldiery we'll stifle We'll confiscate all Melbourne town Its coffers all we'll rifle. (9)

Critics took exception to the appointment of a Chairman to control the meetings, but Jos. Symes carried the objections further in a Liberator editorial of 23 May 1886:

Melbourne Anarchist Club name is one of the grimmest jokes conceivable. A Club must be an organised body with laws, committees, chairman, a certain order of doing things, mutual restraint of members, it could not exist without government of some sort.

It may be Home Rule, personal rules, autocracy, etc. etc., but rule there must be or no club or society of any sort, no business firm, no kind of united action, bad or good can exist.

Whatever the objects of the Club -- and from what we know of its promoters, we believe them to be good -- it is ridiculous of them to give themselves a name, the sense and meaning of which they must necessarily violate every step. (10)

However, no rules, laws, committees (except for Secretary), chairman or particular order of management were ever recorded for posterity. True, the Club had prospectus of objects in general, had ideas for an Association and apparently ties with the Anarchist International but these actions appear of little consequence.

The Melbourne Punch described the members as loafers, drunkards and thieves, etc., and brought forth a stinging reply in verse. Needless to say the press then, as now, never permits challenge to its own veracity. However, the verse is recorded in no. 1 issue of Honesty (11) and can be reprinted upon a later occasion.

Besides the Co-operative Home and Co-operative Printing Coy, which printed Honesty, the Club conducted a "Melbourne Co-operation of Laborers No. 1", mainly to combine in purchase, production and exchange based on the cost principle. Labour notes, bearing no interest, would be issued for circulation among members and the public. The capital of the co-operation was to be owned by the whole, each member having an equal share. Taxation by the "organised State" was to be evaded or minimised as far as possible.

It is clear in principle that the Club attempted to establish co-operatives within any field of common purpose amongst its members with common ownership of the enterprise. This was not altogether dissimilar to many of the co-operatives under modern government legislation.

There were sixty-five people recorded as being present at one time or another; twenty-nine are re corded with only one appearance, five on two occasions, one on each of four and five occasions, and three on six occasions, leaving twenty-six who were more regular. Of course, some recorded may not be members.

David A. Andrade and William C. Andrade, brothers, were foundation members, the latter moving to Sydney shortly after joining. The former appears as the Secretary of the Club from forming to finish. Both brothers were in the library and bookselling businesses. W.C. Andrade represented the Melbourne Anarchist Club at the Fourth Annual Conference of Australian Free thinkers in Sydney.

Carl Arndt was an eccentric land surveyor until the 1920s. Robert Beattie and D.W. Brookhouse lectured often. J.A. Andrews was a gentle poet, philosopher, editor, compiler of the Handbook of Anarchy, correspondent to United States, Australian and the local press. Other members included W.A. Gregory, John D. McMillan, Peter J. McNaught, George C. Newberry, Fred P. Upham, John W. Fleming and John White.

Monty Miller had fought at Eureka Stockade in 1854, John White and his father were active in the Chartist uprisings of 1848, Fred P. Upham had experiences among the Chicago anarchists, J. White, F. Anstey and J.W. Fleming brought English experience.

In other directions, John White, J.W. Fleming, S.A. Rosa, G.C. Newberry were to lead the unemployed. Carl Arndt and Kauffman were members of the German Social Democrats (Verein Vorwarts Socialestene, Victorian Branch). John Brunton and P.J. McNaught were members of the Land Nationalisation Society, C. Drake a Secretary and D.A. Andrade Acting Secretary of the Free Discussion Society. T.O. Roper was Architect of the Hall of Science, Marshall Lyle, barrister, and Bernard O'Dowd, poet, must have been friendly. J.K. Dunn wrote the pamphlet Sweating and generally most were capable of addressing a meeting on some subject or another. They were a not inconsiderable force of men of varied experiences, knowledge and education who were supplemented by outside lecturers.

All this during a period when little other political activity took place. Monty Miller continued political work in Victoria and Western Australia and was to be jailed for six months at eighty-five years of age by W.M. Hughes, under the War Precautions Act as a member of the I.W.W. He died a Communist. Frank Anstey became a Labor member of the Federal Parliament. W.A. Trenwith, who may not have been a member of the Anarchist Club, became State and Federal Member of Parliament. J.W. Fleming continued leading May Day Processions as an anarchist for another fifty or sixty years.

L.D. Petrie and S.A. Rosa founded the Social Democratic League which was the predecessor of the Labor Party and which supplied the bulk of the Labor Party's platform of 1891. The former joined William Lane's party to Paraguay where he died, the latter continued activity into the First War Conscription Campaigns in Sydney.

All subjects were orders of the day. Anarchy, philosophical and otherwise, economics, land, capital, labour, co-operation, State Socialism, etc. etc., were discussed. Generally most were dissatisfied with the existing form of society and its government; they varied as to the remedy, some for voluntary co-operation, some state socialists, some socialists and others communists.

There seems to be a general belief that we are opposed to all Governments. Certainly we are opposed to all existing forms of government. But you see, the only government we know is a mixture of subjection, roguery and robbery. Governments of today govern the people whereas our Government is a government of the people, for the people.

We are credited with a passion for destruction but I should like our opponents to note what we would destroy -- theft, slavery, misery and starvation of body and mind. The doctrine of Anarchism is almost identical with the doctrine of advanced Socialism, what some people call, scientific Socialism.

Life without Equality and Fraternity is a lie as black as hell. And where is the government in the world where they are supreme. Nowhere and they are only possible under the conditions of Socialism -~ Anarchists would govern by conscience although they might use and advocate force to ensure an earlier emancipation of Mankind. (12)

Thus the older school of philosophical anarchists were faced with growing body of believers in the use of force and the older body of believers in voluntary cooperation were facing a growing number of believers in economic organisation by the State or the people in joint ownership.

Hence we see one group printing a leaflet at the Radical Printing Works, Hamilton, N.S.W., and signing it "Anarcho-Communists, Melbourne". This is one illustration of the division. Another was the constant public addresses by Fleming, Petrie, McMillan, Andrews on Socialist subjects. S.A. Rosa, Petrie and others had in July 1889 formed the Social Democratic League.

Thus the very organisation created the intellectual field in which the minds of members blossomed. Perhaps J.A. Andrews may be left to describe the reasons for the break-up of the Anarchist Club.

Andrews in two articles of 18 and 25 October 1896 in Firebrand (13) analysed the reasons for the split in the Melbourne anarchists. He described "the so called individualist maintaining that liberty was property and property was liberty". He said they admitted "legal" property was authority, because it violated their own idea of property. By "legal" property they meant the privilege of holding land idle, of acquiring rent, property and interest.

The Communists on the other hand thought that authority was property and property was authority.

The Anarcho-Communist idea was no property. They claimed simple freedom without privilege and subject to no limitation. It will be seen that Communism is the only state of society in which there is any certainty of people in general having according to their works.

Thus "the idea of reconstructing society on the direct principle of 'to each according to his works' was easily conceived; but when the means of practice were sought for, a serious difficulty arose".

He then traced the "inherent equity" of exchange and said "Communism itself could scarcely offer a more infamous spectacle".

Andrews then declared that the Individualist idea of a single issue of notes by the collective community organised as a single co-operative association was to transform the "Individualist" society into a Liberal Social Democracy.

Between these schools of thought, the Club foundered, the one half becoming the Social Democrats of the day, the other to continue as anarcho-communist. Monty Miller was a classic example at the founding of the Communist Party.

Thus the wide differences between the Communist theory and the Social Democrats' beliefs were nurtured in the Anarchist Club. The problems which divide the world today were those which divided the Anarchist Club.

Reason today is not the real test. It is nice to be critical from academic shelter some seventy-five years later. The proper perspective is to consider also the conditions at the time of these activities.

Certainly the educational opportunities of today were not available then, neither were there the better economic standards of today. Actual poverty and degradations were the seed-beds from which their politic moralities sprang.

Few gained from their political endeavours and in fact most suffered severely. W.M. Hughes, the critic of Crusts and Crusades, appears to have given vent to childish retaliation for the very unfavourable impressions J.A. Andrews had of him. History does not disprove Andrews' views.

This story of the Melbourne Anarchist Club is not complete, through lack of opportunity, but nevertheless endeavours to give the Club its proper place in Victorian radical history - in my view a very important place.

author: rezgar2
title: The Brazilian Victory: Left Unity and Digital Autonomy
content:
Rezgar Akrawi : Lula's victory offers an experience worth studying and learning from. It demonstrates the possibility of cooperation among left-wing forces despite their differences, while recognizing the other factors that contributed to the result.


The left does not need to erase its diversity in order to unite. It needs to turn that diversity into an organized and effective force, strengthen its independence across all five pillars, and pursue the struggle for freedom, equality, and social justice while developing democratic, humanist socialist alternatives to capitalism.


































Author







Rezgar Akrawi




رزكار عقراوي


























    Submitted by 

rezgar2

 on October 29, 2026
  

























































































































































































































Rezgar Akrawi




The leftist leader Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva secured a historic victory in Brazil’s presidential election on October 25, 2026. The result came amid intense political and social polarization and the growing influence of the far right in Brazil and across Latin America, backed by the American far right led by Donald Trump.




The significance of this electoral victory extends beyond Lula securing a fourth term. It also lies in the political and organizational experience that helped make it possible, above all the ability of diverse left-wing and progressive forces, with different programs and ideological outlooks, to forge a broad electoral alliance around common ground in confronting the far right.




A Broad Left-Wing and Progressive Alliance Despite Differences




Lula contested the election with the support of the ‘Brazil Ready for More’ alliance, comprising seven left-wing and progressive parties organized into two party federations and two separate parties. The ‘Brazil of Hope’ federation brought together Lula’s Workers’ Party, the Communist Party of Brazil, and the Green Party. The second federation united the Socialism and Liberty Party, which includes socialist and radical-left currents, with the Sustainability Network. The Brazilian Socialist Party and the Democratic Labour Party also joined the alliance, alongside supportive social movements and trade unions. Lula ran with Geraldo Alckmin of the Brazilian Socialist Party as his vice-presidential candidate.




The importance of this alliance lies in its ability to bring together communists, socialists, the radical left, social democrats, and Greens despite their disagreements over capitalism, the role of the state, and the limits of social reform. These forces agreed on common electoral objectives while preserving their identities and organizational autonomy.




This is one of the most important lessons of the Brazilian experience. Left unity does not require ideological or organizational uniformity. It means being able to work together on common ground while respecting pluralism and differences.

 Disagreements over Lula’s economic and social policies will naturally persist, including among the forces that supported him at the ballot box.




Unity Does Not Mean Abandoning Criticism or Autonomy




The Brazilian experience raises an important question for left-wing forces around the world. Why do ideological and organizational differences become barriers to cooperation, despite so much common ground, even when these forces face shared political and class challenges?




Pluralism among communists, social democrats, the radical left, environmentalist and feminist currents, and independent leftists can be a source of strength and intellectual and political richness, provided it is managed democratically and constructively, without monopolization, exclusion, or claims to possess the absolute truth.

 Unity does not require abandoning criticism or offering unconditional acceptance of the policies of governments led by left-wing and progressive alliances.




Confronting Capitalism and the Far Right Requires a Broad Social Front




The victory demonstrated the importance of connecting the defense of democracy, rights, and freedoms with the economic and social demands of working classes and poor and marginalized communities.




Lula drew broad support from lower-income groups and proposed expanding social assistance, improving living conditions, and defending democratic institutions.




Confronting capitalism and the far right therefore cannot be confined to elections and party alliances. It requires sustained mass organizations in workplaces, neighborhoods, universities, trade unions, and social movements, together with policies that tackle class inequality and improve the lives of the majority.




Digital Autonomy: The Fifth Pillar of the Left’s Independence




The Brazilian election revealed the growing importance of the digital sphere in political struggle. Social media platforms, algorithms, and artificial intelligence have become powerful tools in the hands of capitalist interests for shaping public consciousness and steering political debate.




During the campaign, Lula’s supporters submitted complaints and evidence supporting allegations that Meta, the company that owns Facebook, Instagram, and other platforms, showed digital bias in favor of his opponent. The company acknowledged “technical problems.” The dispute reached Brazil’s electoral court, which issued a ruling requiring Meta to apply equal standards to the candidates.




The problem is not confined to Brazil. During Colombia’s most recent presidential election in 2026, journalistic investigations uncovered coordinated accounts and AI-generated fake videos targeting the left-wing camp, as well as shortcomings and bias in the platforms’ oversight of political advertising and content.




In Germany, Elon Musk, the owner of X, publicly endorsed the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) during the 2025 election. He used his platform to promote the party’s positions and host its leaders, while several studies found a clear bias in the reach of the party’s content on the platform.




Proving deliberate algorithmic bias is difficult because proprietary algorithms give capitalist corporations exclusive control over information about how they work and how content is ranked, amplified, or restricted. Without transparency, independent public and legal oversight, and access to the data needed for investigation, it is difficult to determine whether bias arises from algorithm design or deliberate intervention. Companies can easily attribute such problems to a ‘technical glitch’!




The Brazilian experience also highlighted the importance of combining three interconnected arenas of struggle: mass struggle on the ground, legal action to hold digital platforms accountable and regulate their operations, and organized digital activism. Mass mobilization in the streets was accompanied by legal challenges against Meta and the development of a wide-ranging digital campaign that used social media effectively to reach millions of voters. 

This experience shows that the digital left’s struggle cannot replace grassroots struggle. It can reinforce and complement it.




This is where digital autonomy emerges as the fifth pillar of the left’s independence, alongside ideological, organizational, financial, and media autonomy. Genuine political independence is no longer possible without a meaningful degree of autonomy over digital tools, platforms, and infrastructure, the protection of data, and the capacity for mass communication and organization free from the monopolistic control of capitalist corporations and major powers.




Digital autonomy does not mean withdrawing from digital platforms. It means using them today with a critical, progressive awareness while working to develop open-source, democratically governed digital alternatives and to build and strengthen independent technical capacities within the left.




A left that fails to develop its digital autonomy and technological tools will remain at the mercy of its class adversaries in one of the most important arenas of contemporary political and social struggle.




Lessons for the Left Worldwide




The Brazilian experience cannot be reproduced mechanically. Every society has its own conditions and balance of class and political forces. The Brazilian approach to building alliances and working together can nevertheless offer valuable lessons.




The unity the left needs is neither a single party nor a centralized leadership imposing its vision on everyone. It is flexible, democratic cooperation among diverse forces, grounded in common programs, respect for autonomy and pluralism, and meaningful participation by the grassroots, young people, and women.




Such cooperation can be developed locally, regionally, and globally through different left-wing fronts and alliances on the ground, as well as digital left networks and internationals that contribute to the exchange of experience, coordinate shared initiatives and struggles, and work toward progressive digital alternatives.




Lula’s victory offers an experience worth studying and learning from. It demonstrates the possibility of cooperation among left-wing forces despite their differences, while recognizing the other factors that contributed to the result.




The left does not need to erase its diversity in order to unite. It needs to turn that diversity into an organized and effective force, strengthen its independence across all five pillars, and pursue the struggle for freedom, equality, and social justice while developing democratic, humanist socialist alternatives to capitalism.

author: 张皓翔
title: The Dislocation of Vendémiaire (II): The Illusion of National Economics and the Polarization of Political Economy【葡月的错位（二）国民经济学的幻象与政治经济学的极化】【A commentary on the French riots between September and October】
content: This essay, titled The Dislocation of Vendémiaire, explores the theoretical and practical contradictions within contemporary capitalist society, using the socio-political unrest in France as a backdrop. Grounded in Marxist philosophy and dialectics, the author critically examines the illusion of national economics and the polarization of political economy. By distinguishing between "national economics" (which obscures exploitation through material comfort) and "political economy" (which reveals the deep alienation of social relations), the text argues that modern digital capitalism has stripped workers of their "wealth of real relations" (现实关系的财富). The essay articulates a fundamental shift from the "first struggle" (economic demands for wages and welfare) to the "second struggle" (reclaiming the autonomy of labor production and resisting the reduction of human beings to mere production factors). Ultimately, it posits that the recent French protests represent a historical "dislocation"—an attempt at the second struggle without the necessary political foundation of the first.

title: The Dislocation of Vendémiaire (Part I): The 21st-Century Breakthrough Actors and Ideological Collusion【A commentary on the French riots between September and October】
content: This article takes the French student-led protests and unrest between September and October 2026 as its point of departure. It rejects the mainstream interpretation of the movement as a broad multi-class alliance of diverse demands, and instead argues that it reflects a deep internal differentiation and fragmentation of the proletariat under digital capitalism. While affirming the student group’s role as a “quasi-proletariat” and an early outpost of struggle, the article contends that the movement remained at a pre-Marxist spontaneous stage because it lacked a scientific program and the integration of an advanced party. It proposes “actual control over the production of labor power” as the core criterion for class analysis and describes the movement as a “dislocated” struggle shaped by an ideological collusion between bourgeois narratives and the movement’s own political weaknesses.

title: Chapter 24: The Transformation of Surplus-value into Capital
content:
Harry Cleaver's study guide to Marx's Capital volume one, chapter 24.

The employment of surplus-value as capital = accumulation of capital.

Although net revenue (sales minus costs) = surplus-value, it takes the form of money. It only becomes capital when invested in more means of production and in the hiring of more labor.

For this to happen annual production must include: whatever new means of production that are needed to replace worn-out means of production (depreciation), new means of production that can be bought by the net revenue or surplus-value, new labor power (workers) that can be hired and new means of subsistence to sustain them.

The availability of new labor-power implies wages that "suffice, not only to maintain [the existing working class], but also to increase its numbers."

"The cycle of simple reproduction alters its form and, to use Sismondi's expression, changes into a spiral."
